title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: You're seeing clear measurable productivity gains at Electric Boat, particularly significantly increased earned hours in both the second and third quarters of the year.
epigraph.author: Phebe N. Novakovic, Chairman and CEO, Q3 2026 Earnings Call (October 30, 2026)

web_blocks.html: General Dynamics runs two distinct contracting engines under one corporate roof [1]. Across Marine Systems, Combat Systems, and Technologies, procurement follows the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), multi-year appropriations, and Foreign Military Sales (FMS). Through 9M 2026, consolidated revenue split 60.9% fixed-price ($25,680 million), 32.2% cost-reimbursement ($13,565 million), and 6.9% time-and-materials ($2,896 million) (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q, Note B) [1]. Within Marine Systems specifically, 42.9% of 9M 2026 sales ($5,985 million of $13,963 million) is fixed-price alongside 57.1% cost-reimbursement ($7,977 million). Cost-reimbursement deals shield against overruns on early Columbia-class engineering and GDIT tasks, while fixed-price lots (mature Virginia-class blocks, Abrams/Piranha vehicles, and Gulfstream jets) let GD keep productivity gains—or absorb rework and EAC charges if suppliers or labor slip (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q) [1][10].

In Aerospace, Gulfstream sells direct through a factory sales force to corporations, ultra-high-net-worth buyers, and sovereign fleets [6]. That direct model bypasses third-party dealers and captures full retail pricing [6]. Customers wire non-refundable milestone deposits during the 18-to-36-month build cycle. Those deposits finance work-in-process inventory and convert to revenue upon FAA/EASA certification and delivery [1][6]. Afterward, Jet Aviation's global FBO and MRO network captures recurring revenue from inspections, cabin refits, and fuel.

The largest operational friction in GD's unit economics is sub-tier supply-chain synchronization [10]. Electric Boat relies on hundreds of sole-source nuclear suppliers for castings, valves, and propulsion parts. When one valve or hull section arrives late, shipbuilders face costly out-of-sequence work. Workers install surrounding systems and later tear back into compartments, compressing margins from 9%+ toward 7.0%–7.9% [1][10]. In Aerospace, Gulfstream relies on partners like Honeywell for propulsion and avionics. Engine bottlenecks or certification delays temporarily trap cash in inventory ($9,232 million at year-end 2025) [1][6].

web_blocks.html: To see how General Dynamics converts defense and business-jet sales into cash, the waterfall below scales every audited FY2025 income-statement and cash-flow line per $100 of revenue [1][11]. Stripping $924 million of depreciation and amortization out of direct costs ensures zero double-counting when bridging from sales to EBITDA, EBIT, and free cash flow [1][11].

web_blocks.takeaway: Reconciled cleanly to the FY2025 Form 10-K with zero D&A double-counting: direct costs ex-D&A ($43,675M) and G&A ($2,595M) leave $6,280M EBITDA; deducting $924M D&A leaves exact 10-K operating earnings of $5,356M (10.19%). Net earnings of $4,210M converted into $5,120M CFO (122%) and $3,926M FCF after $1,194M capex [1][5].

web_blocks.mechanism: Paired sole-source UK nuclear submarine construction (Astute & Dreadnought classes at Barrow-in-Furness) and U.S. combat vehicles with long-term multi-year Ministry of Defence / DoD funding commitments, investing heavily in apprentice academies and dry-dock automation before volume ramped.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Built an order backlog exceeding £75 billion with steady 9%–10% underlying EBIT margins and 90%+ free cash flow conversion as submarine production cadence stabilized.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Sovereign nuclear shipbuilding rewards patient upfront capex and workforce training; however, Q3 2026 Form 10-Q MD&A discloses that Marine Systems' +80 bps margin lift to 7.9% was aided by a favorable adjustment on the Virginia-class Block IV program nearing completion, while 42.9% of 9M Marine revenue sits on fixed-price terms and Electric Boat faces active cost-accounting subpoenas [2][4].

web_blocks.title: EAC Sensitivity, Aerospace Warranties & Capital Intensity

web_blocks.html: Unit-economic leverage appears fastest when clean-sheet Aerospace programs pass peak R&D and enter volume production, though hidden warranty and mid-cabin supply friction remain active. Company-sponsored R&D declined from $565 million in FY2024 to $486 million in FY2025 after G800 certification (FY2025 Form 10-K), helping Q3 2026 Aerospace operating margins expand 120 bps YoY to 14.5% across 40 deliveries (119 in 9M 2026) [3][6]. However, G400 FAA certification has shifted into late-2026+, the newly announced super-midsize G300 (replacing the Israel-built G280) requires fresh R&D, and business-jet warranty liabilities climbed from $656 million at year-end 2025 to $691 million at October 4, 2026 as 9M 2026 warranty expense rose 11.9% YoY to $113 million (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q, Note J).

Working Capital & Milestone Billing Mechanics: Gulfstream jets take 12 to 24 months to build, and Navy submarines take 5 to 7 years per hull. Because of those long cycles, working-capital discipline decides whether earnings turn into free cash flow [11]. Navy progress payments and jet customer deposits fund most work-in-process inventory. Still, delayed aircraft handoffs or foreign billing milestones swell unbilled receivables ($8,380 million at FY25) and inventories ($9,232 million) [11]. When deliveries accelerate—such as Q3 2026's 40 Gulfstream handoffs and $1.7 billion CFO (139% of net earnings)—that cash releases rapidly [12].

Contract Mix, EAC Adjustments & Risk-Sharing: Across GD's 8,000+ active contracts, cumulative catch-up Estimate-at-Completion (EAC) adjustments are a material quarterly profit lever. Per Q3 2026 Form 10-Q Note B, net favorable EAC adjustments added $44 million to operating earnings ($0.13 diluted EPS) in Q3 2026—down from $57 million ($0.17 EPS) a year earlier—and $137 million ($0.40 EPS) in 9M 2026. That includes a favorable completion adjustment on Virginia-class Block IV in Marine Systems, while Note B warns that variable consideration on a large international Combat Systems tracked-vehicle contract ($1.2 billion unbilled) could prove lower than estimated [1][7][10][11].

Capital Expenditure Intensity & Payback: FY2025 capex was $1,194 million (2.27% of revenue), and Q3 2026 capex reached $481 million [11][12]. Those outlays fund Electric Boat and Gulfstream capacity rather than maintenance bloat, supporting ROIC above 13% [11][12][13]. Out of every $100 of FY2025 sales, GD converted $8.01 into net income and $9.74 into operating cash flow [1][11]. Subtracting $2.27 of capex left $7.47 in unencumbered free cash flow per $100 of revenue [1][11]. That 7.47% FCF margin funds dividends, debt reduction, and share repurchases from internal cash [11][12].

book_paragraphs: To understand how General Dynamics turns a $220 billion backlog into spendable cash, you and I have to trace two completely different business models side by side. On the defense side, General Dynamics sells to sovereign buyers under the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Look at the 9M 2026 Form 10-Q contract mix: 60.9% of consolidated revenue ($25,680 million) is fixed-price, 32.2% ($13,565 million) is cost-reimbursement, and 6.9% ($2,896 million) is time-and-materials. Even inside Marine Systems, 42.9% of 9M 2026 revenue ($5,985 million) is fixed-price. Cost-plus work—like early engineering on the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine or classified IT modernization at GDIT—protects the company from losing money on first-of-a-kind technology, but it caps margins in the high single digits. Fixed-price production lots—like mature Virginia-class blocks, Abrams tanks, and Gulfstream jets—are where operating leverage and rework risk live.

Gulfstream's distribution model is a textbook cash-flow flywheel when certification runs on time. Instead of selling through middlemen, Gulfstream's factory sales team signs direct contracts with corporate flight departments and sovereign buyers. Those buyers wire milestone deposits 18 to 36 months before delivery, essentially helping finance the $9.23 billion inventory sitting on General Dynamics' balance sheet at year-end 2025. When the jet clears FAA and EASA certification and rolls out of Savannah, revenue and high-teens incremental margins drop straight to the bottom line, followed by decades of Jet Aviation aftermarket service.

Why, then, does Marine Systems earn 7.0% to 7.9% instead of 10%? The culprit is sub-tier supply-chain friction. Building a nuclear submarine requires thousands of specialized, radiation-hardened valves, castings, and hull forgings from small domestic machine shops. When a sub-tier part arrives three months late, Electric Boat's welders and pipefitters have to work out of sequence—installing equipment around missing components and tearing back into compartments later. That rework destroys labor efficiency. On the Q3 2026 call, Phebe Novakovic highlighted the turning point: "You're seeing clear measurable productivity gains at Electric Boat, particularly significantly increased earned hours in both the second and third quarters of the year."

We see a direct historical parallel in BAE Systems in the United Kingdom. When BAE built the Astute and Dreadnought nuclear submarines at Barrow-in-Furness, early supply-chain and workforce bottlenecks compressed margins until apprentice academies and automated dry-dock facilities matured—at which point EBIT margins stabilized in the 9% to 10% range with 90%+ cash conversion. Electric Boat is walking that exact same learning curve today.

Look at the reconciled FY2025 waterfall to see how cleanly the consolidated economics hang together with zero double-counting of depreciation. Out of $52,550 million in audited revenue, direct product and service costs totaled $44,599 million—or $43,675 million excluding $924 million of depreciation and amortization—and G&A took $2,595 million, generating $6,280 million of operating EBITDA. Deducting the $924 million of D&A ($680 million PP&E depreciation plus $244 million amortization) leaves exact 10-K operating earnings of $5,356 million (10.19% margin). After $314 million in net interest, $61 million in other income, and $893 million in taxes, General Dynamics generated $4,210 million in net income and $5,120 million in operating cash flow. Subtracting $1,194 million in capex produced $3,926 million in free cash flow.

Just as important are the hidden unit-economic frictions beneath those headline numbers. On the Aerospace side, company-sponsored R&D stepped down from $565 million in FY2024 to $486 million in FY2025 after G800 certification, helping Aerospace margins expand 120 basis points to 14.5% in Q3 2026—yet G400 certification slid into late 2026+, the newly announced G300 creates fresh development spend, and product warranty liabilities climbed from $656 million to $691 million through October 4, 2026 as 9M warranty expense rose 11.9% to $113 million. Meanwhile, in Marine Systems, Q3 2026 MD&A reveals that the 80-basis-point margin gain to 7.9% benefited from a favorable adjustment on the Virginia-class Block IV program nearing completion, while company-wide favorable EAC cumulative catch-ups contributed $44 million ($0.13 EPS) in Q3 and $137 million ($0.40 EPS) in 9M 2026.

Look closely at that $100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall in Chapter 3, because every penny reconciles directly to the audited FY2025 Form 10-K. Out of every $100 of FY2025 revenue ($52,550 million), $83.11 goes to direct product and service costs excluding D&A, $4.94 goes to G&A ($2,595 million), and $1.76 goes to depreciation and amortization ($924 million)—leaving $10.19 in audited operating earnings ($5,356 million). After net interest (-$0.60), other income (+$0.12), and taxes (-$1.70), GD brings $8.01 to the bottom line as net income ($4,210 million).

Now watch what happens on the cash flow statement. Adding back the $1.76 per $100 of non-cash D&A and adjusting -$0.03 for working capital and deferred taxes yields $9.74 of operating cash flow per $100 of sales ($5,120 million, or 122% net-income conversion). Subtract $2.27 for capital expenditures ($1,194 million)—dry docks, cranes, and Savannah completion hangars—and you are left with $7.47 of pure, unencumbered free cash flow ($3,926 million) for every $100 of sales. The only catch, as we saw in the $8,906 million unbilled receivables line at October 4, 2026, is timing and EAC realization.

Contract structure is where good defense analysts earn their keep. On a cost-plus submarine development contract, the U.S. Navy reimburses allowable costs plus a negotiated fee, protecting Electric Boat from catastrophic inflation overruns—though poor schedule performance still compresses fee percentages. On a fixed-price commercial Gulfstream jet or mature Combat Systems vehicle contract, GD keeps every dollar of efficiency it squeezes out of the assembly line, but also absorbs the pain if sub-tier castings or avionics arrive late.

Understanding that split explains why Q3 2026 Aerospace margins jumped 120 basis points to 14.5% as G700/G800 learning curves kicked in, while Marine Systems margins stayed at 7.9% while absorbing out-of-sequence shipyard labor.

Let us also check capital intensity, because high-capex industrial businesses can look profitable on an income statement while starving shareholders of cash. In FY2025, General Dynamics spent $1.19 billion on capital expenditures—just 2.27% of revenue. Even as Electric Boat expands dry docks for Columbia-class submarines and Gulfstream scales G800 and G400 completions, total capex sits comfortably around 2.3% to 3.0% of sales, leaving roughly 7.5% of every revenue dollar as genuine free cash flow.

When you hear management discuss progress payments and milestone billing on future earnings calls, you now know exactly what to listen for: whether inventory and unbilled receivables are releasing cash back onto the balance sheet as deliveries cross the finish line.

Understanding that working-capital rhythm—progress payments funding work-in-process, followed by milestone cash release upon delivery—is the key to forecasting General Dynamics free cash flow across quarters.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The 51% fixed-price / 44% cost-reimbursement split is a deliberate risk barbell. Cost-reimbursement absorbs R&D and first-of-class risk on Columbia-class submarines, while fixed-price production lots capture learning-curve margin expansion once designs stabilize.
